# Acceleration and Sparse Structures

Also called: Sparse Acceleration, Cache-Based Rendering, Visual Hull Sampling

## Overview
Acceleration and Sparse Structures optimize the computational bottleneck of NeRF training and rendering by replacing dense, uniform ray sampling with sparse data structures or constrained sampling volumes. This family solves the problem of excessive MLP invocations and memory bandwidth limitations inherent in standard volumetric rendering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Adaptive Ray Sampling](8870-adaptive-ray-sampling.md) by explicitly discretizing the scene into grids or hulls to enable memory-bound lookups rather than iterative density-based decisions, and from [Scene Representation and Architecture](11368-scene-representation-and-architecture.md) by focusing on inference-time speedups via caching rather than training-time representation efficiency.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family rely on the principle of **sparsity** or **constraint** to reduce the number of points queried by the neural network.
1.  **Constrained Domain:** Instead of sampling over the entire scene bounding box, points are restricted to a subset of the volume. This subset is either defined by geometric constraints (visual hull) or data-driven occupancy (sparse grids).
2.  **Lookup over Computation:** High-frequency or pre-computed data is stored in discrete structures (voxel grids, hash tables, or caches) to replace expensive MLP forward passes during inference or specific training stages.
3.  **Interpolation:** Continuous values (density, color, radiance) are recovered from discrete grid cells using interpolation (nearest-neighbor, trilinear) or basis function combinations.

## Subtopics

### [Zip-NeRF Training Procedure](9538-zip-nerf-training-procedure.md)
A two-stage inverse rendering optimization that uses neural radiance caches to estimate incoming light. It differs from siblings by decoupling cache initialization from joint physical model optimization and using a control variate (Fast Cache) to correct bias in radiance estimation. Choose this for physically-based inverse rendering where accurate lighting estimation is required.

### [VaxNeRF](11379-vaxnerf.md)
An acceleration strategy that restricts ray sampling to the **visual hull** $V$, the maximum volume compatible with object silhouettes. It differs from siblings by using a single MLP with uniform sampling inside $V$, eliminating the need for coarse/fine sampling stages or adaptive sampling. Choose this for multi-view scenes with clear foreground-background segmentation to achieve 2–8x speedups.

### [FastNeRF](11399-fastnerf.md)
A rendering architecture that factorizes the 5D radiance function into position-dependent and direction-dependent components stored in sparse 3D grids. It differs from siblings by explicitly decoupling spatial and directional data into separate caches to avoid polynomial memory explosion, enabling 200Hz rendering. Choose this for real-time inference where MLP invocations are prohibitive.

## Background
The need for acceleration in NeRF stems from the $O(N)$ cost of MLP evaluations per pixel. Early works like [FastNeRF](11399-fastnerf.md) introduced grid caching to replace MLPs at inference time. [VaxNeRF](11379-vaxnerf.md) leveraged geometric priors (silhouettes) to prune empty space during training. More recently, [Zip-NeRF](9538-zip-nerf-training-procedure.md) extended caching to inverse rendering, addressing the bias introduced by approximating incoming radiance. These methods build on the foundational [NeRF](52-nerf.md) framework but diverge in how they handle the volumetric integral.
